answer.label: Not Dwight D. Eisenhower — an anonymous 1948 joke
answer.authorDates: In print by 21 October 1948 · originator never identified
answer.sourceLine: The earliest version Quote Investigator has located ↗ ran in a classified advertisement in the Amarillo Daily News on 21 October 1948, credited to nobody more specific than “some crazy guy.” Eisenhower’s name was first attached in Esquire in December 1969 — the year he died — and QI states it has found no instance of the line in his writings or in an interview.

source.excerpt: Things are more like they are right now than they ever have been.
trail: 1948, Amarillo. A classified advertisement in the Amarillo Daily News of 21 October carries the line, ascribed to “some crazy guy” — the earliest instance Quote Investigator has found ↗, and already in circulation before Eisenhower took office in 1953.

1962–1966, anonymous. QI traces ↗ the saying through a Texas column by Cayce Moore, a March 1963 column by Rod Riggs in the Ames Daily Tribune with no attribution at all, an epigram collection crediting a fictional character, and a Minnesota paper crediting an unidentified Houston speaker. No president anywhere in it.

December 1969, Esquire. The first known credit to Eisenhower, in the year of his death: “Things are more like they are now,” Eisenhower once said, “than they ever were.” QI records it ↗ with no supporting evidence from Eisenhower’s own record.
Today, on Wikiquote. The line is absent from the curated Eisenhower page ↗ and instead sits in the talk page’s Unsourced list ↗, with no citation attached.
source.excerptNote: This is the wording of the earliest appearance Quote Investigator has located ↗, and it is not a presidential utterance — it is a joke dropped into a Texas real-estate classified, ascribed only to “some crazy guy.” The familiar modern forms (“…than they ever have been”, “…than they ever were before”) are later drift; QI notes the form of the expression evolved over the decades.

author.name: Dwight D. Eisenhower
author.kicker: About the man it’s pinned on
author.heading: Who Eisenhower actually was
author.bio: Dwight David Eisenhower (born October 14, 1890; died March 28, 1969) led the Allied Expeditionary Force in the Second World War, directing the campaigns in North Africa and Normandy, and rose to General of the Army. He then served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. His plainspoken, folksy public manner is almost certainly why this piece of circular nonsense drifted onto his name — but the line was already in print before he took office, and it appears nowhere in his documented record.

misattribution.heading: Two presidents, no evidence
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook case of a joke shopping for a spokesman. The saying circulated anonymously for about two decades, then acquired a president, then acquired a second one when the first stopped being topical.

items.why: The line was already in print in 1948, before Eisenhower took office in 1953, and the earliest credit to him that Quote Investigator locates ↗ is a December 1969 item in Esquire — the year he died — reading: “Things are more like they are now,” Eisenhower once said, “than they ever were.” QI states it has found no direct evidence in Eisenhower’s writings or in an interview that he wrote or spoke the saying.

The earliest Ford credit QI records ↗ is a 1983 Connecticut newspaper, with New York magazine repeating the Ford version in 1986. QI finds no evidence that Ford said it either, and treats the switch as the same ascription being transmitted without skepticism.

Whole Grains: A Book of Quotations printed it under his name in 1973 — “Things are more like they are now than they ever were before. DWIGHT D. EISENHOWER” — and Robert Byrne’s 1982 collection did the same, per QI ↗. Aggregators still reproduce the attribution with no citation at all: The Quotations Page ↗ offers only “Dwight D. Eisenhower, 34th president of US 1953-1961 (1890 - 1969)” and no source.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody knows who first said it. The earliest appearance Quote Investigator has found ↗ credits only “some crazy guy” in a 1948 Amarillo newspaper advertisement — the presidential names were attached decades afterwards.

context.heading: Why a nonsense line needs a president
lead: A tautology is only funny if someone solemn says it. On its own, “things are more like they are now than they ever have been” is a scrap of wordplay — the kind of thing that turns up in a joke column, a graffiti collection, or a real-estate ad trying to be charming. Attach it to a head of state and it becomes a punchline about how leaders talk, which is a far more portable joke. That is the engine that moved this line.

The paper trail Quote Investigator assembled ↗ shows it happening twice. For roughly two decades the saying circulated with no famous name on it at all — ascribed to “some crazy guy,” to a fictional character, to an unnamed speaker in Houston. Then it landed on Eisenhower, and once quotation anthologies printed it that way it stopped being checkable. In the 1980s the same line was handed to Gerald Ford, with no more evidence than the first time.
context.detailsSummary: The attribution drift, year by year
detailsBody: 1948 — A classified advertisement in the Amarillo Daily News (21 October) prints “Things are more like they are right now than they ever have been,” ascribed to “some crazy guy” — the earliest appearance Quote Investigator has found ↗.

1962–1966 — QI tracks it through a Texas column by Cayce Moore (jokingly credited to a “Committee in Washington”), a March 1963 column by Rod Riggs in the Ames Daily Tribune with no attribution, a 1963 epigram collection crediting a fictional character, and a Minnesota paper crediting an unidentified speaker in Houston.
1969 — It appears in a University of Virginia graffiti collection under “Word Play.” In December, Esquire prints the first known credit to Eisenhower.

1971–1982 — The poet Howard Nemerov passes it on hedged (“President Eisenhower is reported to have said…”); Whole Grains: A Book of Quotations (1973) prints it flatly under his name; sports columnist Ira Berkow (1974) says Ike used it while president; Robert Byrne’s The 637 Best Things Anybody Ever Said (1982) credits Eisenhower.
1983–1986 — A Connecticut newspaper gives the line to Gerald Ford, and New York magazine repeats the Ford version. QI finds no evidence for either president.
context.pull: “Some crazy guy” is the only attribution the earliest known version carries.
